HALIMOS (Sea Orache)

Also known as damasonion, also erymon,
also brittanike, also rabdion, also
basilike; the prophets [call it] "Hermes' foundation," like
flesh; also "Osiris's diadem";
also "crown of Pan"; also "sacred oar."
Pythagoras [calls it] anthenoros; the Egyptians
[call it] asphoin; also asontēri; also asello-
ērē; also asaraphē; the Romans call it
labukium; also ampoullakia.

The shrub is a hedge-plant, similar to buckthorn,
though not thorny, and the whole plant
is rather pale, and its leaves,
like those of the olive, are broader, however,
and softer. It grows mostly
in places near the sea, among hedges
and fences, and its leaves are
eaten. A drachma's weight of its root,
drunk with honey-water, helps against
pulled muscles, ruptures, and colic.

ALIKAKKABOS (Winter Cherry / Bladder Cherry)

Also known as dirkaion, also
"mad down," also
doryknion; the Romans [call it]
apollinaris minor, or
herba vaticana; also
ouagem; the Dacians [call it] koikol-;
the Africans [call it] kakkabum.
It has leaves similar to nightshade (strychnos),
though broader. Its
stems, as the plant
grows, become like bladders,
reddish, round, equal
in size to grape berries, and
garland-weavers use them,
weaving them into
garlands.
It has a cooling power,
so its leaves, applied as a poultice,
are good for
erysipelas and creeping sores,
mixed with barley meal.
A marvelous thing besides...

Applied crushed, it treats styes (aigilopia) and headaches,
and relieves burning fever; it is worn for parotid swellings
when crushed and applied as a poultice; and its stalk, too,
[mixed] with egg white, with silver [leaf?], and with rose oil, is good against erysipelas
and [...] against styes, when bound on.

in wool, so administered. Its fruit, too, is able to purge jaundice,
being diuretic. The herb is also pressed for its juice and dried in the shade, for
storage, against much mustiness.

III.

ARTEMISIA MONOCLONOS, ARTEMISIA
THE OTHER, POLYCLONOS

Some call it toxitis, others Ephesia, others parthenike,
others hypolysson, others Anactoria, others sozousa,
others leia, others leukophryx; the prophets call it "blood of man,"
the Romans ullentia, others serpullum,
others herba regia; the Gauls call it ponem, the Dacians zuzustrum.

It grows for the most part in places near the sea, resembling wormwood,
but larger and broader. One kind of it is vigorous, having broader leaves
along its stems; the other is whiter, with small, fine, strong-smelling flowers,
and it blooms in summer. Sometimes among those growing inland there is
a thinner-fruited plant with a single stalk, bearing a small flower,
pale in color, delicate, which they call artemisia.

Both kinds warm and thin the body. When boiled, they are suitable
for women's sitz-baths, to bring on menstruation, the afterbirth,
and the fetus, and for uterine obstruction and inflammation of the womb,
for breaking up stones, and for retention of urine. The herb, applied as a
plaster in quantity on the lower abdomen, brings on menstruation within a month.
The juice extracted from it, mixed with myrrh and applied as a pessary,
draws out matter from the womb; and when drunk as an enema it promotes
hair growth in the same manner.

APARINE

It has an unripe-grape-like fruit; some call it "philanthropon" (man-loving); some call it "ixos" (bird-lime). It has many long, four-angled, rough stems, with leaves set around at intervals in a circle, like those of madder. The flowers are white; the seed is hard, round, somewhat mottled, with a navel-like depression in the middle. It is also tolerated for use with milk-curdling; shepherds use this plant instead of a strainer for milk, to catch the hairs floating in it. The seed and its juices are drunk, and the leaves when pressed for juice are drunk with wine against persistent inflammations; it is also made into compresses for the ears when mixed as a poultice. The plant, mixed with fat/lard, disperses scrofulous swellings.

ASARON

It is also called wild nard. The prophets called it "limaron"; the Egyptians named it "keras" (?); the Romans [call it] "peressam"; some call it "blachaton"; the Etruscans [call it] "knoumi"; some [call it] "nardourikes"; the Gauls [call it] "baikar"—a plant [used] for garlands, also called "staphylle." It has an earthy [root] with stems that are somewhat rough between the leaves, flowers that are purple, thin, and fragrant; its roots are used like black hellebore, having the smell of cinnamon. It grows in rough and dry places.

The root of this plant, boiled in water, helps with ruptures, spasms, chronic difficulty of breathing, and difficulty of urination. It also helps menstrual disorders and is given after childbirth, administered with wine. Being astringent, it also [helps] in such cases; it is useful for headaches, inflammations, and bruised or swollen conditions, and it strengthens... There is also [another kind] which... [illegible]
[illegible]

Also called chamairōps, also "dryïsken chros,"
also teukrion; the Romans call it tri-
gōminon; the Gauls call it kuerkia,
ereinon. It grows in rough
and rocky places; it is
a small shrub, a cubit high, having
small leaves similar in
shape and form to oak leaves, bitter; its flower is
somewhat purple and small. One should
gather it always when the fruit is forming into clusters.
It has a warming power. When drunk
with water it helps
against spasms, coughs, and an enlarged
spleen; for those with difficulty urinating
and poor digestion it brings on
menstruation and expels embryos;
when drunk together with vinegar it also helps
those with ascites when taken with wine
and applied as a poultice. Ground fine it
can also be formed into pills
as prescribed, and it cleanses
old sores when applied with honey; mixed with olive oil
and applied as a black ointment it stops
discharge from the eyes, and when smeared on
it is warming.

It also helps with hardenings and wounds, and
checks herpetic sores when applied as a poultice with honey.

DILL

Some call it pêganon, others aniketon; prophets call it "seed of the dog-headed one," likewise "hairs of the dog-headed one." The Egyptians call it the seed of Hermes... the Romans call it anethum, the Africans sikkiria, the [illegible]... dwellers.

Dill is well known, diuretic, warming, good for the stomach,
good for the stomach, and aids digestion. It should not be taken in excess [illegible] together with the antidotes,
corresponding to the sharp-flavored anise. Its root, boiled, is given with milk
just as [illegible] of dried dill: of the flowering tops and of the fruit
the decoction, when drunk, [relieves] milk disorders, griping pains, and intestinal [troubles,]
being very effective; it stops looseness of the bowels and persistent vomiting,
promotes urination, soothes hiccups, and dulls
the eyesight and the generative faculty when drunk continuously; it is useful [illegible]
useful also is its decoction as a sitz-bath for women's uterine troubles,
and its seed, when applied as a plaster, is said to stop warts (condylomata).

VII.

ASTER ATTICUS (Attic Starwort)

Also called asteriskos, also called asterion, also called boubonion, also called ophthalmos; the Romans [call it] inguinalis, the Dacians rathibida.

It has woody stalks bearing at their tips a purple flower, sometimes pale yellow, like the head of chamomile, surrounded at the top by narrow little leaves; the leaves around the stem are somewhat long and hairy. It is suitable, applied as a poultice, against inflammations of the groin while fresh; and when dried, taken up in the left hand by the sufferer and bound around the groin, it stops the pain.

AMARAKON (Marjoram) [text describes Anthemis/Chamomile]

Also called anthemis, also called leukanthemon, also called parthenion, also called chamaimelon, also called chrysokallis, also called malabathron, also called anthos pedinon; the Romans [call it] "soliseculum," also "millefolia"; the Tuscans "cautam"; the Africans "thamako"; the Gauls "vignita"; the Dacians "douodala."

Its leaves resemble those of coriander, fine and thin; its flowers are white around the edge, with a yellow center; it has a strong smell and a bitter taste.

When the dried material is drunk mixed with honey, like epithymon, it draws out phlegm and bile, and benefits those with asthma and those suffering from melancholy. This herb, apart from its flower, is also beneficial when taken as a drink for asthmatics and those suffering similarly. Its decoction serves as a sitz-bath for a womb that is irritated and inflamed. It is also applied as a poultice, together with its flowers, against erysipelas and other inflammations.

VIII.

AMBROSIA (Botrys)

Some call it botrys, some call it botrys artemisia, the Romans call it "cuprum milvaticum," others call it "apium rusticum," the Egyptians call it "merse." It is a small shrub of great beauty, with leaves like those of the wormwood, growing around the shoot of the stem; they are small, like those of rue, the branches around it bearing much seed, like small clusters, which never wither. It is sown like poppy seeds; its root sends out many shoots in Cappadocia, and it is used for garlands. It has an astringent power over discharges, and when applied as a poultice it is repellent.

WORMWOOD (Apsinthion)

The Egyptians call it "somi," the Romans "apsinthium rusticum," or "the bitter pontic one." The best kind is that growing in Pontus and in Cappadocia, on the mountain Taurus, among the growing plants.

It has a digestive power, and it purifies those suffering within, in the stomach and bowels, driving out bile. It is also diuretic, and when drunk beforehand with a bit of Celtic nard it helps against loss of appetite, and it cures jaundice when drunk continually each day in a cup along with three cyathi [measures], taken also for relief, with honey, against drowning victims and those being strangled, when drunk with wine; and against indigestion and poisoning.

It also helps against the sea-dragon's sting, and for those with quinsy it is applied as an ointment mixed together; for dimness of sight and the surrounding region likewise, and also [for] [illegible]... its decoction is useful for excessive [inflammation], and with honey-wine it serves as a poultice for painful eyes [illegible]... as a remedy it is applied to the hypochondria and the [illegible]... stomach; for those suffering chronic illness it relieves them when combined [illegible]... myrtle oil suits the stomach, and rose oil [illegible]... for dropsical patients mixed likewise with soda and nitre and [illegible].

There is also prepared a wine called "wormwood wine," especially in Italy, around the Propontis and Thrace; and it is used for the purposes already mentioned. People drink it regularly when free of fever, and otherwise always drink a toast of it, believing that in summer it promotes health. It is also thought that when woven in among garments stored in chests, it keeps them from being eaten by moths; and when rubbed on the body together with oil, it prevents gnats from settling on the skin.

Some call it abrotonon, some wormwood (apsinthion), some Herakleion,
some ankona, some apogalon, some merikon,
some choloptoion, some thelyphthorion, some
apsinthiomenon, some prokampylon; the prophets [call it]
nevraphoinikos; some kynanchitis; the Romans
[call it] absinthium ponticum; some call it
lythamnos, a tree-like plant with whitish
small leaves, like wormwood from Seriphos, growing around rocky places,
all of it bears a corymb-like tip,
golden in color, appearing in summer, fragrant,
somewhat bitter in taste. The
Sicilian kind seems to be of this sort, but there is another, coarser
one called "matodes," with thin stems, like
wormwood, growing abundantly in Cappadocia and Galatia,
in the part toward Asia, and also at Hierapolis in
Syria.

The seed of these plants, taken with water
and crushed raw and drunk, helps against orthopnea (difficulty breathing),
ruptures, convulsions, sciatica, difficulty urinating, suppression of
menstruation, and serves as an antidote to deadly
poisons when mixed with wine and applied as a liniment.
Burnt together with olive oil, it drives away pests;
when fumigated and drunk with wine it benefits those in pain;
it specifically treats spider and scorpion bites; it also helps
inflammations of the follicles when boiled with henna oil
and applied as a poultice with bread, it dissolves
and tumors; mixed with honey it is beneficial;
it is also mixed into the preparation of laurel oil.

X.

ARGEMONE

Some call it anthemis, others oinone, others homonoia, others anthos pelinon; the Romans [call it] livornia, others concordialis, others pergalia; the Gauls [call it] korna.
Argemone resembles the wild poppy and the anemone; it differs in having its head somewhat flattened above... [and in] not being purple like the poppy, and it has a round root. Then it exudes a saffron-colored [juice], which [when drawn off like] opium produces... a cleansing effect on argemon (a disease of the eye) and on cataract (nephelion), and it soothes inflammations when the leaves are applied as a poultice.

ANOTHER ARGEMONE

Some call it artemone, others arsela, others sarkokolla; the Romans [call it] argemonia.
This one too resembles the wild poppy in its leaves. It has the property, when fresh and ground fine and applied, of healing inflammations of the eyes and of treating cuts. It is also good for dysentery sufferers when drunk with water; it is adhesive for wounds and inflammations of the sinews. Likewise, applied externally, it is effective for spasms and pains. It is also suitable for those bitten by venomous creatures when taken with wine.

There is a small kind and a large kind. Both are resinous and have diuretic properties; when burned as incense they drive away wild beasts. Their fruit is fragrant, sweet, warming, and diuretic, and is taken for chronic coughs and flatulence. The juniper is called "black"; its leaves are pungent, so that when applied as a poultice or drunk—both the leaves themselves and their juice mixed with wine—they are effective against snakebite. The bark, when burned and applied with water, clears up skin eruptions (leprosy); and the sawdust of the wood, when drunk, is purgative/expels [worms].

The root is about the size of an olive, or larger, like a bulb,

pessary for several months; and when applied as a plaster, they

They grow in shady places and around moist ground. Their stalks are black,
smooth, and glossy; the leaves resemble fern, small and smooth. The underside of
the leaves has lentil-like marks arranged opposite one another along the stalks. They
bear neither stem nor flower; the roots are of no use.

A decoction of the herb can help those suffocating with asthma,
jaundice, and difficulty in urinating. It also breaks up stones, settles the bowels,
and helps those bitten by dogs; it clears phlegm from the stomach, and
brings on the menses — it brings on the menses — and dissolves bile, and helps
with the coughing up of blood. It is also applied as a poultice against the bites of
venomous creatures, and against alopecia (hair loss); it thickens scrofulous swellings,
disperses abscesses, scurf,
and watery discharges, mixed with lye, with ladanum, myrtle oil, and wine,
used generally as a cleansing wash. It also makes roosters and
quails more pugnacious when mixed into their feed.

Of pimpernel there are two kinds, differing from one another in the color of the flower. The one having a blue flower is called the female, while the one with the red flower is called the male. Both are shrubby plants, spreading over the ground, having leaves set upon four-sided stems; the leaves are small and somewhat rounded like those of a small grape-cluster, and the fruit is round. Both kinds are soothing and anti-inflammatory; they help draw out splinters and are useful as a nasal rinse. They relieve toothache if poured into the nostril opposite the aching tooth. They clear away pain when mixed with Attic honey, and help with dimness of sight. Drunk with wine, they help those bitten by vipers, as well as people suffering from dropsy and liver ailments. Some say that the one with the blue flower helps reduce swelling of the spleen, while the red-flowered one, when applied as a poultice, causes irritation.

XVI.

Some call it katarchousa, others Libyke, others
archibellion, others alkeibiadion, others onoche,
others porphyris, others medousa, others salyx,
others noneas; the Africans call it bouïnesath.
Its leaves resemble those of lettuce,
rough, dark, numerous, spreading out in all directions
from the root, pressed close to the ground, forming a clump.
It has a root about the thickness of a finger, of a
blood-red color, which grows in the ground and
stains the hands when touched. Its flowers are purple.
It grows in rich soil. The root is
astringent and, when mixed with wax and oil,
is applied to heal wounds that occur spontaneously; for
erysipelas it is applied mixed with barley meal, like a plaster, and cures it; it also treats
skin eruptions and leprosy, when ground together with vinegar and applied.
Applied as a pessary, it also brings about abortion.
Its decoction is given
to those suffering from jaundice, kidney disease, and spleen disease,
and to fever patients, mixed with honey-water. Its leaves,
drunk with wine, check diarrhea.
Perfumers also use the root for
fixing the scent of perfumes.

Right margin: "Ankusa etera; anx(ousa) ysa etera"

Others call it alkeibiadion, and the "lip-herb" (cheiles) as some name it.
This plant differs from
the first kind in having
smaller leaves, which are likewise
rough; its stems are thin,
bearing a purple-colored
flower tinged with red. Its root is
red, fairly long, tapering to
a point, having
a blood-like color.
These plants grow in sandy places.
Their power, and that of
the leaves, helps those bitten
by wild animals, especially those bitten
by vipers: eaten,
or drunk, or simply touched
to the wound, and even when chewed
and placed in the mouth
of the creature—if one then spits it out,
it will kill the creature itself.

XVII.

ALYSSON

Some call it aspidion, others apophyllon
trachy, others akkysiton, others
call it alyseton.
It has round leaves similar to [cress];
the fruit is like little shields, double,
in which is the seed. Taken, it checks
fevers accompanied by thirst, and
held in the hand or smelled, it does
the same thing. With honey it clears
away freckles and skin blemishes. It is
also thought to cure the madness
caused by a dog's bite, when pounded
and bound as a poultice on the bite,
and when hung up in a house it is
said to be a protection against the evil
eye for both people and animals.
Tied on with a piece of purple cloth,
it drives away disease in livestock.

...growing on the Taurus mountains in Cappadocia,
after the "trumpet-plants" [salpingia];
the local people call it sandonikon, named

ASCLEPIAS

Some call it kission, others call it kissophyllon ("ivy-leaf"). It sends up long stalks... its leaves are like ivy. It has long, fragrant roots, a heavy-smelling flower, and seed like small dishes (lekiskoi). It grows in the mountains.

Its roots are helpful when drunk in wine for those with griping pains and for those bitten by venomous creatures. The leaves are good for malignant conditions of the womb and of the breasts.

AMMONIACUM

Some call it agasyllon, the plant from which ammoniacum comes; others call it ammoniac incense; others call it krithos; the Romans call it "helioustros," that is, "ammoniaca." This is the gum of a kind of giant fennel (narthex) that grows in the region of Cyrene in Libya.

One should choose the kind that is well-colored, free of wood, frankincense-like, clean in its lumps, and dense, having no impurity, with a root-like smell, and bitter to the taste. Such a lump is called "eryma"; the oily, earthy mass that is mixed in Libya with the ammoniac is the juice of a kind of green giant fennel.

It has a softening, drawing, and dissolving power against hardened swellings; it also purges the bowels somewhat, and it relieves pains of the joints and of sciatica. It helps also those with dropsy, with orthopnea (difficulty breathing while lying flat), and with epilepsy, when licked up with vinegar for those with fluid retention, taken with honey, or sipped with barley-water (ptisane).

It brings on bloody urine; it cleanses white spots (leukomata) on the eyes and roughness of the eyelids; it dissolves these when mixed with vinegar and applied. It relieves enlarged spleens and excessive hardenings, as well as calluses around the joints, when applied as a poultice with honey — it may even cause [something, illegible] to come out. It is also good for bruises and sciatica when rubbed on, mixed with soda (nitron) and vinegar, and with oil of henna (kyprinon elaion).

XXIX.

BETONICA · · BECHION (Coltsfoot)

The Romans call it Vettonica. It has leaves similar to wild dock, but larger and hairier, astringent in taste. It sends up a stem that is not large, with a thin and short root. Its leaves are pressed for juice while fresh, and this is gathered up. It has an astringent property, particularly good for ulcers of the mouth and tonsils, and it is useful for leukomas (white spots on the eye) and wherever astringency is needed.

Bechion — some call it rhechion, others petrine, others peganon, others pithion, others pagonagon, others chamaileuke, others procheton, others arkophyllon, others chamaigeiron; the Egyptians call it saar thra; the Romans call it tussilago, others pharphara; others poustoulago; the Bessi call it asa.

It has leaves like ivy, but larger, growing from the root, whitish on the upper side and greenish on the underside, with many angles. It has a stem about a span long, bearing a pale yellow flower in spring, which it quickly sheds — and at that time the stem too — so that some have supposed the plant to be stemless and flowerless. The root is thin. It grows around meadows and in moist places.

Its leaves, when dried and applied as a poultice, are helpful against erysipelas and all kinds of inflammation. When the root is burned and its smoke inhaled through the open mouth, it cures those troubled by a dry cough; it also dissolves abscesses in the chest. And the root, fumigated [and mixed] in dead wine lees, is drunk boiled in hydromel (honey-water).

BLACK BRYONY: BALLOTE, OR BLACK HOREHOUND

Some call it black vine, some "cheiroma," some "boukranion"; the Romans call it [a corrupted Latin name]; others call it "batanouta," others "vitis alba"; the Africans call it "pegrina." Outwardly it resembles a cultivated vine, but more like a wild one, and its stems grow larger than any such plant, and it also takes hold of trees with its tendrils. The fruit is grape-like, green at first, but black when ripe. The root is black on the outside, but box-wood colored within. In the first sprouting, its shoots are eaten as a vegetable. They are diuretic, beneficial for the spleen, and suited for those who are paralyzed. The root has a power similar to that of the iris for the same purposes. It is also used for beasts of burden whose eyes have become clouded. The leaves, plastered on with wine, are likewise applied to sprains. Applied to burns it [relieves them]; it removes warts, and cleanses dirty ulcers when mixed with honey.

Some call it black horehound, some call it another kind of horehound, some "nophna," some "notianoskelin," some "nosprason," some "notheras," some "nochelis," some "nostelis," some "nophrys," some "gnothouris," some "gnotera" — the Romans call it "appioun," others "meditam," others "oukeraria," others "marrubium canoherinum"; the Egyptians call it "asphos," others "aiski"; the prophets call it "blood of Zion." GENTIAN

(Latin gloss: Gentiana)

It is also called "kentaurion rhiza" (centaury root), also "Gallic aloe," also "narke," also "cheironion," by the Dardanians "aloeitis," by the Romans "genneus," also "kikenda," also "kouminalis."
It is thought to have been discovered by a certain king of the Illyrians, Gentios, from whom it took its name. Its leaves near the root resemble those of the plantain (arnoglossos), like sorrel; those in the middle of the stem, and especially those near the top, are more divided and smaller. The stem is hollow, about a finger thick, and about two cubits tall, with joints set at intervals and wider gaps between them; it bears leaves and fruit that is light and chaff-like, long, resembling the long birthwort. It grows in high, shady, and well-watered places.

The root has a warming, astringent power. It helps against the bites of venomous creatures when two drachms of it, or of the flower, are drunk together with pepper, rue, and wine; of its juice, about a drachm is given for the same purpose...

GALEOPSIS (also called "dead nettle")

(Latin gloss: Galeopsis, i.e. "dead nettle")

It is also called "galaiobolon," also "galaiphos"; by the Egyptians "aithophi," by the Romans "urtica labonem" [literally "nettle that does not bite"]. It is a small, toothed shrub. In its stem and leaves it resembles the nettle, but its leaves are smoother and have quite a foul smell when rubbed. Its flowers are small and purple. It grows in hedges, along roadsides, and in waste ground.

The leaves and its juice have a dissolving power against skin eruptions, tumors, scrofulous swellings, abscesses, and growths behind the ears. It should be applied as a poultice twice a day with vinegar to make it effective; the poultice and the decoction loosen such growths beneficially. It is thus used for spreading sores, gangrene, and necrosis, applied as a poultice together with salt.

SAVORY (THYMBRA)
Also called "mountain," also "sheep's," also "themitis," also "wild marjoram," also "ageraton." The Romans [call it] cunila rustica, also thymum, also capra rustica. The Egyptians [call it] sekemmen. THYME (THYMOS)
Also called "thymon," also "white thyme," also "kephalotos," also "epithymis," also "thyrsion." The Dacians [call it] mizela; [another people] call it moutouka; the Romans [call it] thymum; the Egyptians [call it] stephanoi. It is known by everyone as a small shrubby, brushwood-like plant, covered with many narrow little leaves, having small flowering heads that tend toward purple. It grows especially in rocky and poor ground.

It has a warming property. Taken with salt and vinegar, it purges phlegm from the bowels. Its decoction with honey helps those who have difficulty breathing. It expels worms, brings on menstruation, expels the afterbirth and even the embryo [induces abortion], and is diuretic. Mixed with honey and warmed, it is good for bringing up [phlegm] from the chest. It heals fresh swellings and disperses clots of blood. It removes warts and skin growths. Applied with wine and barley meal, it relieves sciatica. It helps those with dim eyesight, and eaten as food it is beneficial; it is also useful for everyday dietary purposes as a seasoning in place of a condiment.

THELYPTERIS (Female Fern) —

Some call it "nymphaea pterinon"; the Romans call it "lingua cervina" (hart's tongue). Its leaves are much like those of the (male) fern, having many outgrowths. Its roots are flat, long, somewhat yellowish within, black in parts; some are broader. When taken with honey they expel flat worms. Taken in wine, about three drachms' weight, they expel round worms. Given to women with brine, they bring on abortion, and if taken by one who is pregnant it injures the fetus. THAPSIA —

Some call it "hypopion," others "pankranon," others "scammonion," others among the Romans "thelytelis" or "ferulago," others "wild ferula." The Africans call it "boidin." It is named "thapsia" because it is thought to have first been discovered on the island of Thapsos. In its whole nature it resembles the giant fennel (narthex), but its stalk is thinner than that one's, and its leaves resemble fennel, somewhat sharp. It has umbels like those of dill at the top of each branch, and the seed is broad, somewhat flat, similar to that of elecampane but smaller. The root is black on the outside, white within, large and thick-barked, and acrid; when dug up fresh it must be treated at once while the root is still moist, being treated with heat so that the cut place remains clean of foul exudate — those who dig it should anoint themselves beforehand. The root, when cut up small, is pressed for its juice by means of a press or similar device, and is dried in the sun in an earthenware vessel of suitable thickness. Those who dig it must take care not to stand where the wind blows the vapor toward them, but rather choose a spot free of wind, for it is said [to cause] blistering of the face and of any exposed parts of the body because of the vapor given off; one must therefore [guard against this] ...

...of the parts, one should proceed thus. The bark of the root has a purging power, and so does the juice; and the sap, drunk with honeyed water, purges both upward and downward. It is suited for purging incorporeal afflictions, chronic pains of the sides, and conditions requiring vomiting; it should be given for such disorders mixed sweetly with food. It also has, after its purging action, a binding power — the sap and the root more than all others of equal strength. Where it is necessary to draw out matter from deep within or to bring about suppuration, this is useful. Hence the juice, when smeared on along with vinegar, and the fresh root rubbed on, thickens the skin; it removes bruises and livid marks — the root or the juice combined with frankincense or wax — but it should not remain more than two hours. The juice, applied with vinegar, is usefully smeared on; it is also applied to conditions requiring treatment around the lung, the side, the joints, or the feet. It is useful also for drawing conditions outward, for those who are not naturally warm from circumcision. "Horse-dock"

Some call it wild dock, the Romans "rumex"-stica; there is a kind of dock, a tall plant growing in low places, in all respects similar, but larger than the smaller dock... When drunk or eaten it relaxes the bowels; applied as a plaster with honey and wax, [the roots], whether fresh or dried, differ in strength. Their roots, whether boiled or raw, when applied as a plaster, heal leprous conditions, lichen, diseased nails; and it is good to first rub the area with vinegar. They also soothe itching; a decoction of them, used as a gargle, relieves toothache when boiled in wine and used as a mouth-rinse. They also disperse scrofulous swellings and parotid tumors when boiled and applied as a plaster with wine; they also help the spleen, applied with vinegar. Some also use the root bound around the neck against scrofula. It also stops a woman's flux when applied crushed. A decoction in wine, when drunk, purges jaundice and expels stones in the bladder; it also brings on the menses, and helps those stung by scorpions.

"Horse-fennel"

Some call it "marathis," others "wild marathon"; the Egyptians call it "sampsou," the prophets "thymarnos," the Romans "feniculum agreste" (wild fennel), others call it "feniculus," others "equinus," others "mium"; the Gauls call it "sistrambo." It is a kind of wild fennel. It bears seed like cachrys (a kind of seed), and has beneath it a fragrant root, which, when drunk, helps those bitten by vipers, breaks up stones, and purges jaundice. A decoction of its leaves, when drunk, brings on milk and purges women after childbirth.

IRIS

The Illyrian iris is likewise called by some Thelypeleke, by others Ourania, by others Kathairon, by others Thaumastos; the Romans call it radix murrica; others call it gladiola, others hypertritis, others Consacra trix; the Egyptians call it nari. It is named from the fact that it resembles the rainbow in the sky (ouranos) by its appearance. Its leaves are like those of the gladiolus but larger, broader, and more glossy, growing opposite each other along the stalk, upon which grow flowers — some white, some yellow, some purple, and some the color of hyacinth. Its roots are jointed, firm, and fragrant; when cut, they are dried in the shade and, strung on a cord, are stored away. The Illyrian and Macedonian kinds are the best, and among these the one with a dense, somewhat stunted root, hard to break, yellowish, and very fragrant, which when crushed makes one sneeze and burns the tongue, is the better one. The second kind is white, somewhat pale in color, and pleasant to the taste when chewed. When aged, all kinds become more fragrant but lose moisture, and they retain a warming power. It is said to cleanse, and when applied as a plaster with white hellebore and sittasion it fills up ulcers with flesh and draws out what is difficult to expel; it thins thick humors, and taken as a drink with honeyed wine it has a power against head-colds (coryza).

Isatis
(Latin: Erica domestica)

Some call it lygion, others gnaphalion [prophetai]; the Romans call it "routa," others call it isatis; the dyers use it. XLVI.

CORIANDER, ALSO CALLED KORION · SMOKE-PLANT, ALSO CALLED FUMITORY (KORYDALLIS)

The Egyptians call it ochion, and it is also known as aphroi goid, a well-known plant with a cooling power; hence, when applied as a plaster with barley-meal or bread, it cures erysipelas and shingles. Taken with honey and raisins, it heals night-blindness, and through these same means cures inflammations and carbuncles. With litharge it dissolves scrofulous swellings and tumors. Its seed, drunk with sweet wine, expels intestinal worms and promotes the generation of seed; but if taken in excess, it dangerously disturbs the mind, so one must be careful not to use too much of it. Its juice, mixed with white lead or litharge of silver and with vinegar-and-rose oil, when applied as an ointment, helps inflammations of the eyelids (or similar swellings).

It is also called korion, and also wild korion; it is also called kapnos (smoke-plant), because it makes the eyes water as if from smoke; it is also called kapneitis, also marmaritis, also kapnogorgion, also small chelidonion (celandine), also peristerion, also kantharis; also chalkokros. The Romans call it leium; it is also called fumaria. The Egyptians call it knyx; it is also called toukoi. ERYSIMON (Hedge Mustard)

Some call it chamaiplion, the prophets call it herakleous, the Egyptians call it alphita, the Romans ergomon or erionem. It grows around cities, on building plots, and in gardens. Its leaves resemble those of wild rocket, somewhat narrower, and its flowers are yellowish at the tip. At the end it has slender, curved, horn-shaped pods containing seed a little like cress or turnip seed, similar also in taste. It helps against inflammations of the face and against catarrh, coughs, jaundice, and sciatica, when licked up with honey. Drunk, it helps against deadly poisons. Applied as a plaster with water, it helps hidden tumors, hard swellings of the breasts, parotid swellings, and inflammations of the glands. It has a thinning effect and generally warms the body. It becomes gentler for treating the blood when soaked in water and boiled, and then eaten with fat, having been roasted and ground into a paste.

SMYRNION

It is also called hipposelinon; also agriolon; also "wild celery"; the Romans call it olus atrum. It is distinct from the other plant properly called "smyrnion," as we shall explain presently. It is larger and whiter than garden celery. The stem is hollow, tender, tall, as if marked with lines, having broader leaves, somewhat reddish, with foliage that whitens in the middle; at the flower-clusters it is three-forked and compact, the seed being black, somewhat elongated, coarse, and aromatic. The root is slender, fragrant, and pleasant to taste. It grows in shady places and in gardens, and it is eaten as a vegetable like celery — both leaves and stems, cooked or raw — and it is also prepared together with fish; by itself it is preserved in brine. Its fruit, when drunk with honeyed wine, induces menstruation; it warms those who are chilled when drunk, and when applied as an ointment it helps those suffering from strangury. The root, too, has the same effects when applied in the same way.

HERAKLEION, OR PANKRATION                    HEMEROKALLES

Some also call this plant "skilla" (squill); but another kind of squill has a root like a bulb, somewhat purple, and fiery to the taste. Its leaves are like those of a lily, but longer. The root has the same power, preparation, and dosage as true squill, and it produces the same effects as the plants of that kind, though the power of this one is weaker than that of true squill. For this reason, when the root is pressed for its juice and mixed with bean-meal and formed into little loaves, it is given with honey-water, beneficially, to those suffering from spleen disease and dropsy.

Some call it "hemerokallis," others "krinon agrion" (wild lily), others "krinanthemon" (lily-flower), others "porphyranthes" (purple-flowered), others "bolbos emetikos" (vomiting bulb), and others "antikantharon." The Egyptians call it "iokry," the Romans "bubuli," and others "lilium marinum." It has leaves and stalks like the lily, but green like a leek. It bears flowers arranged along the stalk, three or four to a branch, resembling those of the lily, beginning to open wide at the tip. Its color is pale; its root resembles that of a bulb, of good size. When this root is dried and combined with honey and placed in wine, it acts as an expectorant and emmenagogue (it draws out phlegm and brings on menstruation). Its leaves, applied as a poultice, soothe inflammations of the breasts after childbirth and inflammations of the eyes. The root and leaves are also usefully applied as a poultice to burns.

GARDEN MINT                                    WILD MINT

Some call it "mintha," others "kalaminthe"; the Romans call it menta, others nepita; among the Egyptians it is called pherorumonthou, others perzo, others makio. It is a well-known plant, having a warming and drying power. Taken as a drink, its juice, mixed with vinegar, kills round worms; it stirs sexual desire, and stops hiccups, vomiting, and cholera when two or three sprigs are drunk with the juice of sour pomegranate. Applied as a poultice with barley meal, it disperses abscesses; placed on the forehead it relieves headache; it soothes swelling and pain of the breasts; it also helps when applied as a poultice to dog bites; its juice mixed with honey-water is good for earache. If placed in a woman before intercourse, it prevents conception; rubbed on a rough tongue, it smooths it; placed in milk, it keeps it from curdling; and it is a pleasant drink for inducing menstruation.

The Romans call the wild mint "mentastrum." It grows with hairier leaves and is in every way larger than the sisymbrium kind, more pungent, and less suited for beneficial use in health.

HELIOTROPION (Heliotrope)

Some also call this plant "scorpiouron" (scorpion-tail), others call it "scorpiouros." It grows in marshy places and by lakes, having leaves similar to the one described before, but rounder, and a round fruit hanging down like little warts. The herb, drunk together with its fruit along with soda, hyssop, cress, and water, can expel round worms. Ground fine and applied as a plaster with salt, it also cures warts.

HEPATOREIOS (Eupatorium / Agrimony)

Some call this plant "eupatorion," others call it "hepatitis"; the Romans call it "holosteon," the Egyptians "oxyon." It is a shrubby plant bearing a single slender, woody, upright, dark stem, somewhat hairy — sometimes larger. Its leaves are divided like those of hemp, mostly into five parts or more, resembling those of cinquefoil or hemp; they too are dark and notched like a saw at the tips. A kind of creeping seed grows in the middle of the leaf, somewhat hairy, bending downward, which when dried clings to clothing. The leaves of this plant, ground fine and applied with old lard, heal the most stubborn sores. In addition, the herb itself, drunk with wine along with its seed, helps those suffering from dysentery, liver ailments, and those bitten by venomous creatures. Some call this plant "artemisia."

WILD CABBAGE · · SEA CABBAGE · ONION

The Romans call it "brassica rustica." It grows for the most part near the sea and in cliff-like, rocky places. It is wilder than the cultivated kind, and is whiter, hairier, and more bitter; its stalk twists like ivy, which is why it is not eaten. Its leaves, applied as a plaster, have the power to close up wounds and to disperse swellings and inflammations.

Others call it sea-cabbage; the Romans call it "coliculus marinus." The plant called sea-cabbage is a kind of cabbage having long, thin, numerous leaves; each of them grows on small branchlets, like those of the rock-rose. It bears a small white fruit; it has a somewhat salty taste and similarly in its general character. The whole plant, when eaten, is most effective at loosening the bowels; the Italians also preserve it in meat [brine/sauce].

As for the many kinds of onion, the ancients and the Romans call it "cepa." The small kind is sharper than the round, the yellow sharper than the white, the dry sharper than the fresh, and the whole one sharper than the peeled and preserved kind. All kinds are irritant and provoke a windy appetite, are expectorant, diuretic, purgative, good for the bowels, able to open obstructions, promote excretions of various kinds including the menses, and act counter to [snake] venom.

It is applied peeled and dipped in vinegar. Its juice, smeared on with honey, is useful for dimness of sight, for white specks and growths on the eyelids, for ulcerations, and for sore throats; mixed with Christ's-thorn it provokes and brings on the menstrual flow when poured in. It is also good against alopecia, and as a poultice for the head and for dog-bites when mixed with salt and rue and honey — which is why it can heal vitiligo when smeared on with an equal amount of ash... It is also used, mixed with bird's... for repairing the soles/glue of shoes.

KYAMOS (Bean)

The Romans call it "faba." The green (unripe) bean is harder on the stomach and more flatulent. A poultice of beans soothes inflammations resulting from blows, and likewise mixed with barley meal it eases swollen and inflamed breasts, being beneficial, and it dries up milk. Mixed with honey it [relieves] tendinous swellings; with meal it disperses parotid swellings. Mixed with rose oil and [applied], it cures prolapses of the white of the eye and checks watery discharges. It is also sprinkled, well pounded with dill, upon [the skin] to prevent excessive hair growth when applied repeatedly; and the shelled, powdered husks, sprinkled on, make plucked hairs grow weak and sparse, and also form scabs. Mixed with barley meal and the oil of privet, applied as a poultice, it disperses scrofulous swellings, and the pod (husk) itself, when split, is applied to these. CRATAEOGONON, OR KRATAIGONON                           CROCUS

It has leaves similar to those of melampyron; several shoots grow from one root, jointed, with a seed resembling millet. It grows in shady and brushwood places, mostly in rocky terrain, and is strongly pungent. It is reported by some that drinking the seed causes a woman to bear male children, if, after her purification, before having intercourse with anyone, she drinks it fasting, in a dose of three obols with two cups of water, for forty days; and likewise the husband should drink for the same number of days.

CROCUS

Castor knows it, as does Cynomorphus; the prophets of the harbor of Heracles also know it. The best is the Corycian, from Cilicia; second is the Lycian, from the Corycus near it, on Olympus in that region; third is that from Aegae in Aeolis. The Cyrenaic and Sicilian varieties are weaker in potency, but juicier and more vigorous in growth, which is why they mislead many people. For medical use, the best is the fresh one, well-colored, not many years old, white, somewhat elongated, whole, full, not having a hollow, airy texture.

When pressed, it stains the hands without being greasy and has a slightly pungent quality — for one that lacks this is either unripe, old, or has been stripped of its essence. This is revealed when crocus paste is mixed in: the genuine kind, when weighed out, balances against a measure of litharge or lead oxide, while the adulterated kind is shown to be dusty by its texture... it should emit fragrance when bent and not crumble when pressed. Thessalus, however, says that it is merely fragrant, and knows it to be dangerous, saying that giving three drachms of it with water is, in truth, diuretic and mildly astringent; therefore it is also used for erysipelas, applied around the area with water, and for rheum of the eyes and similar conditions, it is combined with milk as eye-salves or ear-drops. As for mouth preparations, there is also an unmixed form, the root of this plant, which when drunk with sweet wine promotes urination.

Clematitis — Another Clematitis — Kestron (Betony)

Some call it "epigetes," the Egyptians "philakouon," the Romans "anbouzou," others "olokroum," or "laktoulaktouke." The clematis sends up a reddish shoot, pliant, with a very sharp-tasting leaf, and is somewhat harmful. It twines around trees like smilax (bindweed). Its fruit, drunk with water or honey-water, purges phlegm and bile downward. The leaves, when made into a plaster, remove leprosy-like skin conditions. It is also preserved with fine oil for eating.

...it is drunk with branches while fresh; it grows in dry places.

The other kind is called by some "philetairion," by others "daphnoides," or "polygonon" by others. It grows along the ground; its shoots are small, about the thickness of a rush, and its leaf resembles that of the bay tree in shape and color, but much smaller. Its leaves and stems, drunk with wine, stop diarrhea and dysentery. Taken with milk and rose oil or henna oil, applied as a suppository, it relieves pains of the womb; chewed, it helps toothache. It also helps when applied to the bites of venomous creatures. It is also said to help those...

Kestron (betony) is found in the coldest places. The Romans call this plant "outeponike." It has a thin stalk, somewhat square and rather larger, with long leaves similar to those of rue, having jagged edges, fragrant; it leans upon a long support. Along the long stalk is where the seed grows in a spike, like that of millet. One should gather the leaves of this plant and dry them; their use is for treatment. The root is thin, like that of hellebore, and these cause phlegmatic purging.

It is drunk with honey-water for ruptures, and for conditions of the womb, for suffocation of the womb, in the weight of a drachm, with honey-water or water; and for those bitten by venomous creatures, even three times with wine.

The herb, when applied as a plaster, heals those bitten by venomous creatures. For the same purpose, a dose about the weight of these [seeds/parts] taken with wine is suitable. If someone drinks it beforehand, he will suffer no harm, even if he has taken a deadly poison. It is diuretic and assists the passage [of urine or stone]. It also cures those subject to seizures and the mad, when drunk with water. Taken with oximel (vinegar and honey) to the weight of one drachma, it helps those with liver and spleen ailments. It is given to those with stomach troubles — it should be chewed and swallowed, or sipped mixed with wine. And when four portions are added with hydromel... it helps with consumption as well; for those spitting blood it is combined with honey... The leaves should be kept fresh in an earthenware vessel.

CORN POPPY, APHRODITE'S POPPY, HORNED POPPY

Some call it "oxytonon," the Romans call it "papaver album," the Egyptians call it "panti," because it drops its calyx quickly. It grows among barley in spring, which is when it is gathered. Its leaves resemble chicory, but more deeply cut, smaller and rougher. Its stem is reed-like, upright, and rough, about a cubit tall. Its flower is reddish, sometimes white, resembling the wild anemone's, though its head is more elongated, though less so than the anemone's. The fruit is reddish; the root is long, whitish, bitter, and about a finger thick. Five heads of this, boiled down from three cups of wine to two and given to drink, induce sleep. Taken with honeyed water, as much of the seed as will cover a coin gently loosens the bowels; it is also mixed into honey preparations. The same leaves, applied as a poultice along with the poppy-head, heal inflammations, and a decoction made from them induces sleep.

Some call this one "heraklia." It has a stem about a span tall and very small leaves resembling those of the sparrow-plant. Its fruit is white and foamy. The root is thin, and from it more fruit is gathered once it is fully ripened in summer; if it dries without falling off, it purges by vomiting. A small cup's worth taken with honeyed water is suitable, and is especially useful for such purging in cases of suffocation (choking fits).

Some call this one "paralion," others "wild poppy," others "thalassion"; the Romans call it "fabiolum marinum," the Africans "cissimacesa." It has white leaves, rounded at the edges like those of the wild poppy, with fruit and stem similar to it. Its flower is pale yellow and curved like a horn, resembling that of fenugreek, from which it takes its name. Its seed is small and black, like that of the poppy. The root grows near the surface, black and thick, and it grows in places near the sea and in rough terrain. Its property: the root, when dried and taken with wine up to half a measure, and drunk, treats sciatic and liver ailments, as well as affections of the sides and chest.

There is one kind that is cultivated, grown in gardens, whose seed is made into bread for ordinary use, and mixed with honey is used in cakes. Common to both is a cooling property; for this reason the leaves and the poppy-head, boiled in water and drunk, induce sleep. They are also useful, boiled down, against insomnia, and as a poultice. Three poppy-heads mixed with [something] are suitable against inflammations and erysipelas when applied as a plaster. The heads themselves, boiled until the liquid thickens, make a painkilling remedy effective against sciatica and rheumatic conditions of the joints, as well as disorders of the bowel. Andreas says that if it were not adulterated, it would blind those anointed
with it, saying that its use is fitting for sleep, but otherwise it happens
to be harmful—what is in fact a lie, for experience disproves those who say
it is beneficial, when, upon testing, the effect of its juice is examined.
It is not out of place to describe the manner in which they collect the poppy juice (opos).
Some, pounding the poppy heads together with the leaves,
press them out with a pestle, rubbing them in the sun, and they form
them into lozenges; such is called "mekonion," weaker than
the (pure) juice. Those who collect the juice must do so after the dew
has dried, and mark around with a small knife an asterisk shape,
so as not to pierce through to the interior;
and cutting the poppy heads obliquely at once, only on the surface,
and when what comes forth dries, the process is repeated again. This too
is found to be of use. One must also store it after shaping it into lozenges. Whenever
one cuts for the juice, one must take care not to let it dry out
too much before storing it as a garment(?) of the labor.

ONOGYROS (Anagyris)

Some call it "anagyris," others "akope." It is a shrub-like plant with leaves and branches resembling the chaste tree (agnus castus), tree-like, with a strong heavy odor. Its flower is like that of the cabbage. Its fruit grows in long, somewhat rounded pods, variegated, and hardens around what forms at the top [of the pod]. The leaves of this plant, applied as a poultice, disperse swellings. A drachma's weight of it is given to drink with sweet wine for nausea, and to bring down the afterbirth and menstrual flow. For headache it is applied with wine, and it is also used as an amulet for women having difficulty in childbirth. Its fruit, when eaten, induces vomiting.

[Marginal: onopych-]
ONOBRYCHIS

Some call it "onobrycheilos," others "eschasmene," others "hyperikon," others "korin," others "chamaipitys." The Romans call it "oggata," others "brichzalata," others "nopiga," others "iounkinalem." It is sharp and pungent in taste. Its leaves resemble those of the lentil but are somewhat longer. It has a stem about a span high, with a small flower, and it grows in watery places. It has a property that is somewhat astringent; it disperses tumors, and when drunk with wine it treats strangury, and when mixed with oil it induces sweating.

OROBOS
[Marginal: orobos]
The Romans call it "ervum." It is a well-known small shrub with narrow leaves, having seed contained in pods, growing wild, called the kind from which "orobinon" flour is made, which is also suited for medicinal use. It is heavy on the head and astringent; if eaten it causes hunger [craving?], and is diuretic in effect; it stimulates — [and] harms cattle when mixed with their fodder. A kind of coarse bread ("orobinos") is also prepared from it. Such is its nature.

It whitens and nourishes the skin when sprinkled with water, cleansing it of impurities. It is ground together with roasted barley, the shell removed, then crushed and strained through a fine sieve and stored. It induces good sleep, is diuretic, aids digestion, strengthens the weak, and is eaten as food in a drink after meals.

It purges through the bowels and bladder. It cleanses sores when mixed with honey, and (removes) freckles and blemishes and spots, and stops spreading sores on the rest of the body, and gangrene, and softens hardness in the breasts, and heals animal bites, and bursts open carbuncles and boils when kept in wine; it cures dog bites and snake bites. When applied as a plaster with vinegar, it relieves difficulty in urination and colic and intestinal cramping. It is also suitable as food, about the size of a nut, roasted and dipped in honey. Its decoction, when poured over the body, relieves chilblains and itching all over.

CULTIVATED ORMINON (Clary/Sage):
The Romans call it "geminalis," the Dacians "ormea." PTERIS            ANOTHER PTERIS            POLYPODION

[Pteris:] Some call it pterion, some pterineon, some dasyklonon, some anasphoron, some blechron, some polyrizon; the prophets call it "Hermes' basin"; the Romans call it filix; also lakoulla; the Egyptians call it philikem, haimaonou. It has no stem, no flowers, and no fruit. Its fronds are about a cubit in size, divided and spread out like a wing, with a somewhat unpleasant smell. Its root is black, elongated, with many branches that are somewhat astringent to the taste. It grows in mountainous and rocky places. Four drachms of this root, taken with honey-water, expel broad tapeworms. It works even better when taken with a little black hellebore — about two doses — and it is said to kill intestinal worms in those who take it.

[Pteris etera / female fern:] Some call it nymphaia pterin, others call it thelypteris (female fern). Its leaves resemble those of the (male) fern, but are more numerous and taller; its roots are long, mossy-looking, blackish with a yellowish tinge, having a reddish color. Taken with honey, they expel broad tapeworms; when drunk in wine in a dose of three drachms, they expel round worms as well. Given to women, they cause barrenness, and if a pregnant woman takes it, it brings about miscarriage. Applied below the knees... as a plaster upon damp or moist areas... it is sprinkled upon beasts of burden... The fresh young leaves, used as a vegetable, and when boiled and eaten, soften the bowels.

[Polypodion:] Some call it skolopendrion, others call it pteris, others polyrizon; the Romans call it filicula or "oak-leaf" (quercifolia). It grows on mossy rocks and on shady cliffs, among the mosses, reaching about a span in height. It resembles the fern, somewhat hairy and divided into segments, though not so finely. Its root is hairy, with tendrils like those of an octopus, about as thick as a small finger; when scraped, it is green within, somewhat astringent, but with a slightly sweet taste as well.

NYMPHAEA (Water Lily)

It grows in marshes and standing waters. It has leaves similar to the colocasia (kibōrion), but longer and more elongated, rising somewhat above the water; but most of the plant, from the root itself, remains in the water. The flower is white, similar to a lily; when it has faded it becomes round like the head of a poppy — black, within which is the fruit, which is black, flat, dense, and sticky to the taste. The stem is smooth, not thick, rather large, similar to that of the colocasia. The root is black, rough, club-shaped, and large; it is cut in autumn, and when dried and drunk it helps those with intestinal complaints, taken with wine, and also helps those with spleen trouble. It is also applied as a plaster for pains of the stomach and bladder. The root cleanses skin blemishes (alphos) when used with water, and cures baldness when applied mixed with pitch. The root is also useful against nocturnal emissions, for it checks those who suffer from this affliction — it works for a few days, unless one drinks it continually. The seed does the same thing. It seems to be named from "nymphs," because it loves watery places. It is found in abundance near [a certain river] and in the river of Boeotia at Orchomenus.

THE OTHER NYMPHAEA

Some call this one "Nymphon." This nymphaea too is similar to the one described above, but its root resembles more that of the colocasia; however, it has a white and rough root. Its flower is yellow and glossy. The root and seed are good for women's flux (excessive menstrual bleeding) when drunk in wine. It grows in places near the sea, in the region of the river Peneios.

Some call the narcissus "anygros," others "autogenes" ["self-growing"], others "bulbos emetikos" ["emetic bulb"], and others "lirion." The Romans call it "bulbus morbitarius." Some have also called this flower "lirion," as though it were a kind of crinon-lily. Its leaves resemble those of a leek, but are smaller and narrower; the stem is hollow and leafless, rising more than a span high, bearing at its top a white flower with a saffron-colored center, though in some varieties it is purplish. The root is white inside, round, and bulb-like; the seed, enclosed in a membrane, is black. The finest and most fragrant kind grows in mountainous regions, while the white variety has a leek-like, grassy smell. Its root, eaten after boiling, or drunk, induces vomiting. It is also good for burns when applied with honey, and for cuts near sinews, acting as a plaster that glues wounds together. It relieves sprains of the ankles and joint pains, and when applied as a poultice it soothes long-standing aches; it also removes freckles. Mixed with vinegar, bitter vetch, and honey, it clears impurities from ulcers and hard, undigested swellings; it bursts and cleans out boils and splinters when applied as a plaster made with wheat flour and honey.

The Romans call it "ferula." Green narthex, when eaten, benefits those suffering from stomach ailments and dysentery. It is given with wine to those bitten by vipers. Used as a pessary with wine, it checks excessive menstrual flow. Its seed, taken as nourishment, is beneficial for those who are hungry [weak from fasting], and when applied as an anointment, it checks sweating when mixed with oil. The stalks, when eaten, are good for headaches, and they are also preserved in brine [pickled] for use.

Knekos (Safflower) · Kypairos or Kypēron (Galingale)

[Knekos:] It has long, cut-into leaves, rough and thorny, with stems about two cubits long, also thorny, bearing at their tops heads of considerable size with flowers resembling crocus (saffron). The seed is white and reddish, elongated and angular. Some people use this plant in sauces. The seed, when pounded with honey-water or chicken broth, purges the bowels and benefits the stomach; and when pounded, it softens the bowels. Also, when drunk mixed with almond, soda, anise, and honey, one should take it early in the morning before dinner, dividing it into three or four portions each the size of a royal walnut. It should be prepared in this manner: one xestes of white knekos, three cups of roasted anise seeds (?), one litra of anise, one drachma of foam-of-nitre, forty dates in number. It also coagulates milk; the juice of its seed, mixed with wolf's-bane, also has an effect.

[Kypairos/Kyperon:] Some also call this plant "eryosischoinos," as the Romans call it "aspalathus," and others "kiradikem," others "kyoum." It has leaves similar to leek, but longer, thinner, and harder; the stem is about two cubits or even taller, angular, resembling a rush, not with leaves at the top but with small clusters, and the roots form a pair of tufts, whose use is like that of marsh-reed: elongated, joined to one another, black, fragrant, like Kyperos, bitter. It grows in rough and marshy places. The best kind is the heaviest, the most bitter, and the most abundant, rough, hard to break, aromatic, with some pungency. Such is the kind from Cilicia and from the Cycladic islands.

Its property is warming and opening (anastomotic).

Leukoion (Stock Gilliflower)
The Romans call it "basilion," also "pulla alba," also "viola alba," also "lygustea," also "viola matronale," also "passarina," also "pulli foura."
Its variety is recognizable by its flower, for it is either white, or saffron-yellow, or purple, or blue — all useful for medicinal purposes. Its dried flowers, boiled, are used for sitz-baths for inflammations around the womb and to bring on the menses. When taken up in a wax ointment, they heal cracks on the finger; mixed with honey, they heal mouth sores. Its seed, drunk with wine in a dose of two drachms, when applied with honey also brings on the menses and the afterbirth. Its roots, applied as a poultice with vinegar, reduce the spleen and benefit those suffering from gout.

Sea Leukoion (Sea Stock)
The Romans call it "viola alba marina."
It has the same properties as the previous plant, though it is not as strongly effective.

Ligustikon (Lovage)
The Romans call it "panakes."
It grows mostly in Liguria, from which it also took its name, in the mountain called the Apennine, which borders on the Alps. The local people also call it "panakes," though not correctly, for it resembles the Heraclean panax (opopanax), and its properties are similar in themselves. It grows on the highest, roughest, and most shaded mountains, especially near mountain streams. It has a slender stem resembling dill, and leaves like those of celery, but more tender; they are fragrant and rather slender toward the top of the stem, and more divided; at the top it bears an umbel, and its seed is black, broad, and oblong. The root, when tasted, is pungent and aromatic like that of fennel, and white in color.

or drunk. Combined with this, it helps a customary ailment,
relieving colic and gripes; it is good against pain of the sides
and chest, difficulty breathing, coughing, pneumonia, hip and
joint complaints, feverish chills — taken periodically as has
been said, boiled with honey; and cooked, applied from below,
smeared with honey onto the privy parts up to the anus, as an
application.

The Romans call it "ruta hortensis";
the Egyptians call it "epnubu";
the Syrians call it "harmala";
also called "besasa"; the Africans call it "churba";
it is of two kinds.

Also known as hypericum, also called androsaemon, also
"coris," also called "chamaepitys" by the Romans;
"inderalis," also called "centum nervia," also
"arundinale," also called "rutalco";
also called "rutalcovatica," also "misy";
the Africans call it "chumma-semmaked."

Because of the resin-like substance around its seed,
resembling resin, it is called "tuini." It has small
leaves like rue, a shrubby, brushwood-like plant, rising
to about the height of a hand or three fingers. It exudes a
blood-like fluid from which it is also called androsaemon —
they call it so. It has elongated, rounded pods like barley,
in which grows black seed smelling of resin. It grows on
rough and rocky ground.

It has diuretic and emmenagogue properties; applied, it
is also effective for working purposes; taken with wine
it benefits the hips; it also ripens abscesses within a week
when applied. Its leaves, similarly prepared as a plaster,
are good against burns.

Olive oil also expels worms when applied as a poultice; [it treats] swellings when mixed with honey, and with figs it helps against dropsy; combined with a little flesh[y substance] it is helpful. Likewise it is useful for [illegible] some people [illegible], but others, applied raw and salted, and poured into the eyes, soothe the surrounding pain. Applied as a poultice with barley meal it eases pain, and with rose oil it also helps those suffering from headache. It checks hemorrhages when introduced into the nostrils. For inflammations in the testicles, applied as a poultice with bay leaves, it is beneficial. It also helps against skin eruptions when combined with myrtle wax ointment, and with soda it is useful; when applied around it cures white leprosy (vitiligo). Applied as a poultice together with the same ingredients it removes warts and ant-bite-like growths (small tumors). It is helpful also for lichen (skin disease) when applied with honey and alum. The juice itself, when warmed in a pomegranate rind and applied, is good for earache. When smeared on, it cures erysipelas and herpetic sores; mixed with white lead and rose oil and applied, it heals them. It also counters the odors and acridity from garlic and onions if one anoints oneself with it beforehand. The mountain variety, when eaten much by the kite (bird), and when gathered before flowering for salting, turns reddish, and stains the skin, causing itching and severe inflammation...for the inflamed face and nostrils, it soothes them in this way. They say that the greenery, when scattered, keeps birds away from cultivated land. The one growing in Macedonia along the river Annymos, they say, is deadly when eaten; the mountain region where it grows is full of vipers, and its seed, when drunk, acts upon the internal organs. It is also mixed usefully into antidotes.

The Romans call [the female kind] seminalis minor. It is a small shrub having a single, tender, reed-like stem, with joints set closely together continuously, like those of a rope-plant (spartion), and around the joints small leaves resembling [those of the male plant]. Its root is useless. It grows near watery places. It has an astringent, cooling power, producing the same effects as the previous plant, except that it is weaker.

It grows in the mountains, a shrub taller than a cubit, having leaves like laurel but broader, and when tasted sweeter — similar to a quince apple, yet somewhat more astringent besides. At each point where the leaves emerge there are white flowers, exceeding in number those growing from the root. The root is white and soft, long — this is called polygonaton — hairy, heavy-smelling, about the thickness of a finger. It is useful applied as a plaster to wounds, and it also removes blemishes from the face.

[The juice is collected] cut from parts where the stalks are sprouting; famine [goes unnoticed(?)]. The juice, when dried on its surface, turns saffron-colored. It also brings on menstruation and destroys the embryo, and when applied as an enema it disperses flatulence and hardness in the womb. It is suitable for gout sufferers when mixed with the sap of the wild grape and held under the tongue. It also relieves toothache when placed among the food. Fresh sap applied with oil in the sunlight is good for the eyelids and for hair: it both affects the fine, blond hairs that grow in, and eventually removes all the hairs. With a purple-colored [appearance], the leaves similar to smilax, the seed black, and the capsules hard and thorny. The soft fruit yields juice, as do the leaves and stalks when pounded; dried in the sun, its moisture is used for some conditions because it is prone to putrefaction. The seed also yields juice when pounded dry and hot water is poured over it and pressed out; this pressed juice is always better and more effective against pain than the drink. The green part, when pounded and mixed with wheat flour, is formed into pastilles; this is suitable, [as is] the first extract and that made from the dried seed, for eye-salves against pain and inflammation, and for earaches, and for conditions of the womb, mixed with flour or barley meal, against inflammations and swellings of the eyes and other such things.

The seed itself, prepared, is good against cough and catarrh, and discharge of the eyes and painful conditions, and for women's disorders, and against hemorrhage—about one obol's weight taken with poppy seed, or with honeyed water. The seed is suitable for gout, swollen testicles, and breasts swollen after childbirth, applied as a smooth poultice; it is also usefully mixed into other pain-relieving poultices, and the pounded leaves are usefully mixed into all pain-relieving poultices along with barley meal, and also by themselves. Fresh leaves applied as a poultice relieve pain in all cases; taken three or four times in wine, they cure persistent fevers. CXLIX.

TRAGORIGANON (Goat-marjoram)

It is a shrub similar to oregano or wild thyme in its leaves and twigs. In some places a stronger and broader-leaved kind is found, which some call Prasion, others call it by the name given by Aristhenes, and others call it Smyrnean or Cretan. It loosens the bowels when its decoction is drunk, for it brings down bile. Spanish varieties too, when sprinkled with vinegar, are made into a relish; taken with wine they bring on the menses. It helps also with inflammations of the lungs when taken with honey, and it is given to those who have lost their voice, and it relieves nausea and warmth of the upper abdomen. It also helps swellings when applied as a poultice mixed with barley meal.

TRAGOS, or TRAGEION, or SKORPIOS, or GARGANON

Some call it Tragion, others Tragokeros, others Skorpion, others Garganon; the Romans call it Cornulaca, others Vitouensa, others Irkoulou Dentaria; the Dacians call it Salia; the Egyptians call it Sober; the Africans call it Achchoioueim. Its leaves resemble those of the hart's-tongue fern (skolopendrion); its root is white, thin, and altogether like that of wild radish. It helps those suffering from dysentery when taken as a draught and also when boiled... it yields about ten [parts/leaves]. In autumn the leaves have the smell of a goat, from which it gets its name. It is also good, together with pomegranate rind, for larger inflammations around the anus and for large cavities when boiled with rose oil mixed with honey, applied to spreading gangrenous sores; likewise when mixed with seawater. It is also useful for blisters, creeping sores, and erysipelas, and for bruises, as stated before. For hardened breasts and nipples, when boiled in vinegar and water, it is suitable applied as a plaster.

On Chrysocome:
The plant called Chryseitis is also known as Chrysathemon, also as Amaranthos, also as Diospyron; the Romans call it Jovis barba (Jupiter's beard), the Africans call it Doubath. It is a small shrub having a tuft of hair-like, cluster-shaped growths similar to a sprout of flax. Its root is shaggy, and when tasted it has a flying, hellebore-like quality, not winged like cypress, producing a sweet, somewhat astringent taste. It grows in shady and rocky places. It has a warming and astringent power, and is suitable for liver and lung ailments, when taken with hydromel (honey-water); it also helps as a cleansing agent for the uterus.

On Chrysogonon:
It is also known as Chrysospermon, also as Lapin, also as Linon, also as Origanon, also as Arkophallon; the Romans call it Agriaria. Its leaves resemble those of the oak, and the shrub is dense. Its flower, found all around, is used in making garlands. Its root is similar in shape, rounded, growing strongly within... it helps externally when applied, being effective, soothed with vinegar and ground fine, and applied to shrew-bites.

On Chrysanthon, also called Elichryson:
This too is called Amaranton, as it is used to crown the gods as well. It has a straight, solid stem, with narrow leaves, somewhat resembling the foliage of southernwood, round and shield-shaped, golden-bright, rounded, like clusters. Its root is thin, growing in rough and ravine-like places. Its foliage, when mixed with wine, helps against difficulty urinating, snake bites, sciatica, and uterine issues, also bringing on menstruation, and dissolves clots of blood in the bladder — drunk with wine or honey-wine. It also helps with sciatica and chronic catarrh when given fasting in wine. [It is] mixed with white... and preserved with garments to keep moths away most effectively.

CHRYSANTHEMON
OR CHALKAS

Some call it chrysanthemis, others chalkitis, others chalkanthon, others chalkanthaimon, others call it buphthalmon; the Romans call it acantha, the Thuscans garouleon, the Africans chourzeta. It is a somewhat delicate plant, shrub-like, with smooth stems rising up, and leaves finely divided, and flowers of a golden color shining strongly, round like eyes — hence it has been so named. It grows around cities; its stalks are eaten as a vegetable. Its flowers, crushed and mixed with wax ointment, are said to disperse fatty swellings. For jaundiced patients it also produces a good complexion for a time, when applied after the long exertion of bathing.

CHONDROS

Some call it dikokkon, others call it zea; the Romans call it far. Chondros is made from the so-called "two-grained" zea; it is the most nourishing of foods, like rice, and binding to the bowels, though less easy on the stomach when fresh. When ground fine and applied, it removes leprous conditions of the nails, and it begins to heal incipient aigilops (a kind of eye ulcer) when used as an enema in a decoction. A decoction of it is also suitable to use for the pain of dysentery.

CHONDRILE

Some also call this kichorion (chicory), others call it seris. Its leaves, stem, and flowers resemble chicory, whence some call it "wild seris." The whole plant is more slender. Around its small stalks there forms a gum-like substance, resembling rows of grains the size of a bean, which, when combined with myrrh in a linen cloth about the size of an olive, induces menstruation. The herb itself, when pounded, is preserved in the form of lozenges, and is used after being mixed with honey. These, when dissolved and combined with soda (nitron), scour away stones. The gum also serves to glue hair back on, and the fresh root does the same, when the hair is dipped into it.

It is also known as "katafysis," also "kynokephalion," also "krystallion," also "kynomyia," also "psylaeris," also "Sikeliotikon" by the Sicilians, commonly called by the Romans "silvaticum," also "herba pulicaris" by the Africans, "uargugum." Its leaf resembles that of coronopus, but hairy and longer; the branches are about a span long, and the whole plant is grass-like. Its foliage begins from the middle of the stem; the heads, two or three, are twisted together at the tip, and the seed resembles fleas — black and hard. It grows in cultivated fields.

It has a cooling property and is beneficial, when made into a plaster, for arthritis, swollen glands (parotids), tumors, inflammations, spasms, and headache (mixed with rose oil and vinegar-water); also for intestinal hernias in children and for protruding navels, when applied as a poultice. One should steep a generous amount — about an oxybaphon's worth — in two kotylai of water, and drink it mild throughout; it cools sufficiently.

CHAMAIDAPHNE                CHAMAISYKE                CHAMAIMELON

Those in Alexandria call this plant [Chamaidaphne]; others call it daphneitis, the Egyptians "hydragogos," the Romans "lauriola" ["lyriphola"], others "lalagon," and still others "ousouben." It sends up only shoots, straight and very slender, with leaves like those of the bay (laurel), but much smoother and smaller, bearing a round, reddish fruit growing upon the leaves. Its leaves, when applied as a poultice, help afflictions of the head and stomach in cases of burning fevers. Taken in wine, they check [certain] fluxes. Its juice, mixed with honey, and applied as a salve, helps the eyes; sprinkled on, it does the same thing when so applied.

[Chamaisyke:] Some call this plant "syke," others "mekon," the Egyptians call it "aphyis," others "klosis," others "anisis," and "tetradaktylos," because it lies spread upon the ground. It bears leaves like lentil, flat, similar to purslane; its fruit is small, round in the leaves; it has a flower like that of the fig (syke); its root is of no use. Its properties are useful against the stings of scorpions and the beginnings of a cataract-like dimming of vision; applied as an ointment it is dissolving; it is given to drink for those suffering from dry [ailments/coughs].

[Its leaves] enclosing it, and on the outside there lies around it a round-shaped white, pale, or purple (flower), about the size of a rue leaf. It grows in rough places and alongside roads, and is gathered in spring. The root, the herb, and the flowers all have a heating property. More effective among the varieties for individual purposes is the purple-flowered kind, which common people consider larger, properly called the "eranthemon" (ground-flower). They are therapeutically applied when arranged [as poultices] and when chewed; some people use them mixed with ointment, grinding them with oil for the treatment of periodic (recurring) fevers. The leaves and flowers of each kind are stored, being pounded and made up into small lozenges together with the dried root, to be given whenever need demands. The taste of the herb's one part is sweet, while the other, sharper part is pungent; it should be drunk mixed with wine and honey.

Some call it "golden sceptre," others "ixia." The Romans call it "cardos ularinos," others "pine-cardos," others "lacte-cardos." Drunk with wine it also serves as an antidote against venomous bites; it kills dogs as well, when mixed with [other things] and applied as described.

CHAMAIAKTE (also called "chalus")

CHAMAIAKTE: Some call it heleoakte, others wild akte (elder), others the Euboean [elder]; the Romans call it ebulum, the Gauls dukone, the Dacians olma. It sends up a square, many-jointed stem, with leaves like those of the elder, woolly, and all around similar, heavy-smelling, smaller in a circle, and the long elder — both in its flower and in its fruit — is similar; it has a pith the thickness of a reed. Its property is drying and astringent, inducing sleep. The leaves, when boiled, purge phlegm and bile as a potherb does; the tender shoots, when taken in food, do the same; and its root, boiled in wine and given, dissolves dropsy; and boiled with water it cleanses the womb's obstructions, opens them, and sets right the conditions around it; the fruit does the same as the leaf. Mixed with other leaves it is used as a poultice against swellings, and when rubbed on, it also soothes the hair of the lower parts. Mixed with barley meal it is suitable as a plaster for wounds that need to be drawn together, and for prolapses; it is also applied with goat fat as a poultice.
